boards.title: The pool contains six configurations and ten seeds each

visual.label: Historical sixty-predictor pool on 19,000 evaluation cases

boards.visual_argument: Ten-by-ten blocks organize the measured second-moment matrix by model configuration.

segments.line: Keep the actual configurations in view
segments.say: The empirical pool contains ten fitted instances of each of six configurations. They are the relative-loss MLP, the normalized-MSE MLP, the kernel-conditioned refiner, the Fourier neural operator, the UNet and kernel ridge regression. The paper groups them as architecture blocks, but several are related neural configurations and one is a kernel method. It is more accurate to keep those identities visible than to imagine sixty unrelated neural architectures.

segments.line: Separate weight-fitting cases from evaluation cases
segments.say: For this analysis, the public test block is split into one thousand cases used to fit some ensemble weights and nineteen thousand used to evaluate them. The same evaluation cases are shared across all sixty predictors. Some rows are explicitly hindsight optima computed directly on the evaluation matrix. They answer what this fixed pool could achieve on these cases, and are not estimates of the error of a weight-selection rule tested on fresh data.

segments.line: Every cell describes a pair of complete residual fields
segments.say: The heat map shows the measured second-moment matrix. Each cell aggregates normalized residual inner products over the full evaluation fields. The ten-by-ten diagonal blocks compare seeds of one configuration; off-diagonal blocks compare configurations. The plotted values are second moments, not centered Pearson correlations. Large diagonal values can reflect greater individual error, while large off-diagonal values reflect both lengths and alignment.

boards.title: Averaging more seeds gives diminishing gains in this pool

visual.label: Historical sixty-predictor pool on 19,000 evaluation cases

boards.visual_argument: Measured RMS curves flatten as equal-weight subsets grow from one to ten members within each configuration.

segments.line: Average subsets of the available ten fitted predictors
segments.say: For each configuration, consider equal-weight subsets containing one, two, three, five or ten of its fitted predictors. The RMS curves use every possible subset at each size and can be recomputed from the corresponding submatrices of S. This is a finite-pool calculation. It does not require extrapolating to an infinite number of unseen seeds, and it does not treat the overlapping subsets as independent experimental replications.

segments.line: The curves describe this averaging operation
segments.say: For a subset I of size K, sum all entries in its second-moment submatrix, divide by K squared and take a square root. Then average that RMS value over the subsets of the chosen size. The graph shows those directly recomputed values. It answers how much equal weighting improves within the available configurations. It does not isolate every source of variation in network training, nor does it tell us what a newly designed architecture would do.

segments.line: A flatter curve is evidence about shared residuals
segments.say: The initial gains are followed by relatively small changes as more seeds are added. That pattern is consistent with the strong residual alignment visible in the measured matrix. The block-floor theorem makes the connection quantitative without fitting an asymptotic learning curve. A flattened finite-range curve is not by itself proof of a positive limiting error, and we do not draw an unseen infinite-seed point as if it had been measured.

boards.title: Apply the theorem to the measured entries

visual.label: Historical sixty-predictor pool on 19,000 evaluation cases

boards.visual_argument: The empirical lower bound and the feasible hindsight optimum nearly meet on a common RMS axis.

segments.line: Use minima of entries, with the theorem's normalization
segments.say: Choose e bar squared as the smallest diagonal entry. Take the minimum within-block entry and the minimum between-block entry, and divide each by that same diagonal minimum to obtain the coefficients used in the theorem. Check their required ordering before applying the result. These are conservative entrywise quantities. Replacing them with mean correlations would produce a different diagnostic and would no longer establish the stated lower bound.

segments.line: The empirical lower bound is about 4.814 percent RMS
segments.say: Substitute those measured entries into the six-block, ten-seed formula. The resulting lower bound is about four point eight one four percent RMS. This statement is exact algebra for the measured second-moment matrix, subject to ordinary numerical precision. It says that no global convex mixture of these sixty residuals can do better on these evaluation cases. It is not a population confidence bound and does not constrain predictors outside this pool.

segments.line: A feasible optimized mixture is about 4.876 percent RMS
segments.say: The hindsight convex optimum is about four point eight seven six percent RMS. An independent active-set calculation reproduces the released optimizer's value, and a convexity-based lower bound checks the numerical optimum without relying only on an optimizer's success flag. The gap between the block lower bound and that optimum is about zero point zero six three percentage points. There is little room left for global convex reweighting within this measured pool.

boards.title: Hindsight describes the available hull, not a deployment guarantee

visual.label: Historical sixty-predictor pool on 19,000 evaluation cases

boards.visual_argument: The optimum lies inside the feasible convex hull; learning that point from another sample is a separate statistical problem.

segments.line: The optimization uses the evaluation matrix itself
segments.say: The hindsight optimum is deliberately chosen using the evaluation residuals. Its purpose is to describe the geometry of the available predictions on those cases. If it is already close to a lower bound, a better numerical optimizer cannot create much more room within the same hull. That observation is useful even though the hindsight weights are not a deployable estimate of future performance.

segments.line: Weights fitted elsewhere answer a different question
segments.math: \widehat w_{\rm cal}\quad\longmapsto\quad\widehat w_{\rm cal}^{\top}\widehat S_{\rm ev}\widehat w_{\rm cal}
segments.say: A fitted stack chooses weights on the calibration subset and then evaluates them on the evaluation subset. Its performance depends on how well the estimated geometry transfers between those samples. The paper reports fitted and hindsight rows separately. Their difference can reveal weight-selection cost in this experiment, but repeated study of the same public test block still limits a fresh-sample interpretation of the overall research process.

segments.line: Repeated seeds share cases and therefore share evaluation variation
segments.say: The ten training seeds provide useful replication of fitting variation. They do not create ten independent test populations because the same inputs and target fields are reused. Similarly, thousands of overlapping subsets of the same ten predictors are not thousands of independent training runs. Error bars and conclusions should match these dependencies. A visually narrow band can otherwise suggest much more independent evidence than the experiment contains.

boards.title: The deployed pipeline belongs to a larger estimator class

visual.label: Historical sixty-predictor pool on 19,000 evaluation cases

boards.visual_argument: Coordinatewise affine readouts and residual kernels can leave the global convex hull described by the theorem.

segments.line: The theorem constrains global convex combinations
segments.say: The lower bound concerns one global nonnegative weight vector summing to one. The deployed pipeline is more flexible. Its weights can vary by output coordinate, it can include affine intercepts, and it adds kernel corrections. Those operations are not restricted to the same global convex hull. If that pipeline has a lower measured error, it has not contradicted the theorem or somehow broken a universal limit.

segments.line: A mean-error comparison is not an RMS lower-bound violation
segments.say: There is also a metric distinction. The headline pipeline errors are means of per-case relative norms, while the floor controls RMS error. The mean error of the RMS-optimal mixture is not itself the minimum possible mean error over all convex mixtures. Comparing a pipeline's mean with an RMS floor would therefore cross both an estimator-class boundary and a metric boundary. The tables keep those columns separate for a reason.

segments.line: The useful empirical conclusion is narrower and more actionable
segments.say: The evidence suggests that repeatedly adding similar seeds or improving only the global convex optimizer offers limited gains within this pool. A more promising next experiment changes the residual directions, the coordinatewise readout or the representation supplied to the correction. That is a research decision supported by this dataset, not a theorem that one family of architectures will always win. It gives us a concrete reason to investigate what the kernel can add.

boards.title: A common error component is not automatically irreducible

visual.label: Illustrative component diagram; not a fitted decomposition of these sixty predictors

boards.visual_argument: Common, configuration and seed components separate what the observed pool shares from what another method might change.

segments.line: Shared error is a property of the observed predictors
segments.say: Average the normalized residual functions themselves. Their common component records error that these predictors share. The earlier decomposition shows why it survives averaging, but does not establish why the component exists. Similar training objectives, related representations, finite optimization and properties of the numerical target can all contribute. Measuring a common component is different from identifying its cause.

segments.line: The target is a deterministic numerical map
segments.say: The benchmark target includes finite-element discretization and interpolation onto a regular grid. A surrogate is evaluated against those numerical labels. Even if the labels differ from a continuum solution, that discrepancy does not by itself make them impossible to learn. Calling a shared surrogate residual a solver-imposed irreducible floor would require additional evidence, such as carefully matched refined-mesh experiments. Those experiments have not been performed here.

segments.line: Use the bound to locate the unresolved question
segments.math: \begin{gathered}\text{A floor for this pool}\\\ne\text{a floor for the problem}\end{gathered}
segments.say: The empirical bound has done something useful without answering every question. It has localized the best global convex risk within this fixed pool and separated that issue from the search for a genuinely different residual direction. The kernel analysis now asks how a mean and a representation change the remaining approximation problem. Its theorems will be conditional on a function class, while the numerical experiments test whether the proposed corrections help on the recorded data.
